target_audience: University Freshmen and AP Calculus Students

sections.title: Introduction: Explicit vs. Implicit
lecture_lines: In explicit functions, y is isolated and easy to find.
In implicit relations, x and y are tangled together.
Implicit differentiation is needed when solving for y is hard.
animations: Display the text 'y = x^2' (#FFFFFF) next to a box labeled 'f(x)' (#ADD8E6). An arrow points from 'x' into the box, and 'y' comes out.
Display the equation 'x^2 + y^2 = 25' (#FFFFFF) below. Two circles labeled 'x' (#FFB6C1) and 'y' (#90EE90) appear inside a tangled knot graphic (#D3D3D3).
A glowing question mark (#FFFF00) appears over the knot, which then transforms into a differentiation gear icon.

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Chain Rule Reminder
lecture_lines: The chain rule is the engine of implicit differentiation.
Treat y as a function of x when differentiating.
Multiply by dy/dx after differentiating a y-term.
animations: Show the Chain Rule formula: d/dx[f(x)]^n = n[f(x)]^{n-1} * f'(x) in white (#FFFFFF).
The term f(x) smoothly morphs into 'y' (#90EE90) on the screen, showing d/dx[y^n].
The derivative f'(x) morphs into dy/dx (#FFFF00), highlighting the additional factor produced by differentiating y with respect to x.

sections.title: The Golden Rule: Differentiate Both Sides
lecture_lines: Apply the derivative operator to both sides of the equation.
The derivative of x-squared is simply two x.
Differentiating y-squared requires using the chain rule.
This results in two y times dy/dx.
Remember that the derivative of a constant is zero.
animations: Display x^2 + y^2 = 25. Wrap both sides with the operator d/dx(...) in gold (#FFD700).
Transform the d/dx(x^2) term into 2x (#FFFFFF).
The term d/dx(y^2) flashes in yellow (#FFFF00) to indicate it requires the chain rule.
Transform d/dx(y^2) into 2y * (dy/dx) (#FFFF00), emphasizing the dy/dx term.
Transform d/dx(25) into 0 (#FFFFFF), resulting in the full equation 2x + 2y(dy/dx) = 0.

sections.title: The Algebraic Clean-up
lecture_lines: Now we isolate dy/dx through algebraic steps.
Move all terms without dy/dx to the right side.
Keep the term with dy/dx on the left side.
Divide both sides by two y to isolate dy/dx.
Our final derivative is negative x over y.
animations: Show the equation 2x + 2y(dy/dx) = 0.
The 2x term moves to the right side, changing its sign to -2x (#FF6347).
The term 2y(dy/dx) is isolated on the left, with dy/dx highlighted in yellow (#FFFF00).
The 2y moves to the denominator on the right side: dy/dx = -2x / 2y.
The 2s are struck through in red (#FF0000) and fade out, leaving the final result dy/dx = -x/y (#FFFFFF).

sections.title: Visualizing the Slope on a Curve
lecture_lines: The derivative represents the tangent slope at any point.
Consider the point three comma four on the circle.
Plug these values into our derivative formula.
The resulting slope is negative three-fourths.
The tangent line perfectly matches this calculated slope.
animations: Draw a white circle (#FFFFFF) and label it 'x^2 + y^2 = 25'.
A bright green dot (#00FF00) appears on the circle at the coordinate (3, 4).
Display the formula dy/dx = -x/y and substitute the values: dy/dx = -3/4.
The resulting slope value 'm = -3/4' appears in yellow (#FFFF00) next to the point.
A tangent line segment (#FFD700) is drawn through the point (3, 4) with the calculated slope.

sections.title: Real-World Application: The Growing Bubble
lecture_lines: These techniques are essential for solving related rates problems.
Imagine an expanding bubble where volume and radius change.
Implicit differentiation links these rates of change together.
animations: Display the title 'Related Rates' (#FFFFFF) alongside a translucent sphere (#ADD8E6).
The sphere expands; arrows labeled 'dV/dt' and 'dr/dt' (#FFFF00) appear and grow in size.
The equation V = (4/3)pi r^3 appears, then transforms into dV/dt = 4pi r^2 (dr/dt) (#FFFFFF).
